Japan's exports in October surged 20.5% from a year earlier, snapping a two-month slowdown in shipments, official data released Wednesday showed.
Exports growth beat expectations of economists polled by Reuters that had pegged it at 20%, and it was sharply higher compared to a revised 16.5% in September.
Shipments of semiconductor equipment that have been propping up Tokyo's exports jumped 49.7% by value. Exports of motor vehicles climbed 19.9% year on year.
In terms of destinations, shipments to China rose 13.3%, while they climbed 23.9% to the U.S.
Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth, although a surge in the value of imports of petroleum due to the Iran war has offset some the impact of the exports surge on its economy.
Import growth in Japan for October came in at 21.6%, sharply missing analysts' estimates of 25.8%, with petroleum imports climbing 60.5% by value, even as volumes slipped 0.7%.
Analysts previously told CNBC that the surge in value was because Japan was attempting to switch sources to more expensive American oil as shipments from the Middle East stalled.
Imports of petroleum from the U.S. jumped more than 1,100% year on year by value and 738% by volume. In contrast, shipments from the Middle East dipped 16.5% by volume, while higher prices pushed up import value by 37.7%.

How Insiders Got Rich Before the Opening Bell

Anthropic’s S-1 registration statement lists that history. Series A, C-1, D-1, D-2, E-1, F-1, G-1 and H-1 preferred shares automatically convert into Class A common stock just before the offering closes. A long list of other series converts into Class N shares.
Companies now stay private longer because private money is easy to find. In Q3 2026 alone, Databricks reported selling nearly $5 billion of stock to 136 investors[1] in a single private offering. Once these companies list, the public is buying at the end of a long run-up. Anthropic’s insiders and most existing holders also signed agreements that bar them from selling for 180 days after the prospectus date.

The clearest public-market example of an insider-style return is Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction). When the IPO happens, Amazon’s convertible notes turn into Class N stock at the lower of $2.0928 per share (2023 notes) or $5.0478 per share (2024 notes) and the public offering price. Finnish satellite operator ICEYE made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Italian rocket maker Avio on Tuesday, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defense group.
The deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the US and China.
ICEYE said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.
“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said ICEYE, which intends to fund the offer with cash and debt.
ICEYE has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.
“If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe‘s defense will rise to a new level,” said Finnish defense minister Antti Hakkanen.
Investments in Italy
State-backed ICEYE said it intends to invest an additional €1 billion in Italy over five years after the potential deal is completed, seeking to increase the launch cadence and expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.
Avio‘s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which ICEYE said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.
Speaking at an event in Helsinki, ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.
The deal will need several regulatory approvals, including an official green light from the Italian government as Avio is seen as a strategic asset under Rome’s golden power rules.
The CEO of Italian defense group Leonardo, a key Avio shareholder with an 18% stake, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would examine it, in coordination with the government.
European Champion
The deal would pair Avio’s launch and propulsion capabilities with the satellite manufacturing, constellation operations and intelligence services of ICEYE, which was founded in 2014 and provides radar satellite imagery to Western governments and militaries.
“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities… bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.
The Finnish group said it intends to preserve Avio’s brand, retain its existing workforce and continue its planned investments in the United States.
As part of its push into the US defense market, Avio is building a manufacturing plant in Virginia, which it expects to complete in late 2028.

New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies.
According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia.
Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions, the rule said.
The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models.
U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers.
About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank.
The buildout has come under greater scrutiny as Washington presses ahead with the investigation into Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang left the company that he co-founded in 1993 after reports of several alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to facilitate billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips into China.
The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said.
Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out.
Who are most exposed?
Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers.
More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics.
Restricting access to overseas cloud facilities would weaken the commercial case for further expansion and ultimately weigh on investment from both Chinese and U.S. companies, Fahy said.
"Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle," she said, potentially knocking 0.2 percentage points off Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028.
Thailand, which has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction, is also bracing for tighter scrutiny.

The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%.
October's reading puts U.K. inflation at a one-year high.
Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated.
The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022.
Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996.
The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September.
Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July.

On Friday and Saturday, October 30 and 31, NCAA Division I Cross-Country Conference Championships took place in various locations across the United States. The Javelina 100 Mile also took place in Arizona’s McDowell Mountain Regional Park. Judging by the finish times — and despite heavy rains — it appears the front group of runners sprinted for a full 100 miles. In the women’s race, the victory was decided by a mere 56 seconds — a margin of victory that fills me with empathetic distress.
Then on Sunday, more than 61,000 runners took to the streets for the New York City Marathon. We watched epic throwdowns, including Sweden’s Andreas Almgren victory in his debut marathon, and American Jessica McClain came away with a brilliant runner-up finish over the final strides in the women’s race. These are exciting times to be a running fan.
The races themselves were great — the striving and struggling, camaraderie, mud, and the beauty of trying hard (1). But post-race interviews are always my favorite part of big race weekends. These interviews are often drenched in gratitude for good health and the opportunity to compete, for competitors, and for the people who supported their efforts along the way. We hear about families, friends, and volunteers. Athletes often speak in terms of “we” instead of “I.”
It is perhaps surprising that many of the biggest moments of a runner’s career are accompanied by expressions of gratitude. Instead of keeping the focus on themselves, they direct it to others. They win and are given a platform to speak. Then they use this platform to say, “Thank you (2).”
The Concept
Gratitude is a virtue of appreciation that involves recognizing that we have received some good or benefit. For runners, this “good” can mean the expertise of physical trainers, the company of running buddies, the encouragement of family members, or care from aid station volunteers. This recognition involves actions, thoughts, and emotions (3). If your savings sit at JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction), Bank of America (NYSE:BAC), Citigroup (NYSE:C) or Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC), the syndicated consumer money host told listeners, “you hate your money. You absolutely hate your money.”
He also gave the reason. “The biggest banks are going to pay you 1/100th of 1% on your savings,” he said, while “the US Treasury will pay you 5.51% on your savings.”
On $10,000, that works out to about $1 a year versus roughly $551. That gap is what you give up by leaving cash where it sits.
Howard Is Right About the Banks, and Treasury’s Numbers Back Him
My conclusion: Howard’s attack on big-bank savings rates holds up. His I bond pitch also works, but only for money you can lock away for at least a year. If you put your emergency cash into I bonds, you can’t get it back when an emergency hits.
TreasuryDirect confirms a 5.51%[1] rate on I bonds issued from November 1, 2026 to April 30, 2027. That rate combines a 1.4% fixed rate with a 2% semiannual inflation rate.
The fixed rate matters most, because Treasury says it never changes[1]. Bonds bought from July through October locked in just 0.9% fixed. Buy today and you lock in 1.4% above inflation for up to 30 years[1].
On $10,000, that extra half point adds about $50 a year on top of inflation.
The alternatives pay less. The FDIC’s national average 12-month CD yields 1.8%[2], and the 52-week Treasury bill recently yielded 4.55%. The I bond pays about 3 times the average CD.
Here is an example one-year comparison on $10,000. It assumes the I bond rate holds for the full year and ignores compounding:
Even after giving up roughly $138 in lost interest, the I bond still pays more than the average CD. The interest also escapes state and local income tax[1], and you can put off federal tax until you cash the bond in.
When You Need the Cash Decides Whether This Helps or Hurts
Treasury lets you cash in an I bond only after 12 months[1]. If you cash it in before five years, you lose the last 3 months of interest[1]. Howard said the same thing on air: “You have to own them for a minimum of a year.”
Say your transmission fails in month seven. Your I bond money is frozen, so the repair goes on a credit card that charges far more than the bond earns. Cash you might need belongs in an online savings account. Howard said those accounts can pay “as much as 400 times” what the megabanks pay.
Money you won’t touch for five years is a different story. There is no penalty, and you earn inflation plus 1.4%.
Remember that the 2% inflation piece looks back and resets every six months.
In the year through September, consumer prices rose about 3.7%, roughly double the Fed’s 2% goal. If inflation cools, the rate falls.
If the inflation piece drops to zero, you earn only the 1.4% fixed rate, which is less than today’s average CD. Howard has said he would consider cashing in I bonds in a very low inflation cycle.
His 30-year warning comes with a catch. “From that point forward, I earn nothing. Nothing. Not a penny,” he said. TreasuryDirect pays electronic bonds automatically[1] when they mature, so that risk mostly applies to old paper bonds.

Search referral traffic, the visitors search engines send to Reddit, fell meaningfully in the third quarter, management said on the call. The decline sped up late in the quarter, management said. The shares lost 29.2% on October 30, the day after the call. That marked their largest one-day fall of the past year.
Management said on the call that the drop in search traffic appears to come from Google’s rollout of AI Mode. It said people still want Reddit, and Google is just not sending them there the way it used to. Management also said 80% of Reddit’s monetization happens in its app and among logged-in users. So the search warning on the call was about how many people reach Reddit, not about the ads it has already sold. On the same call, management guided fourth-quarter revenue growth below the third quarter’s pace.
Did Reddit’s Earlier Falls Of This Size Pay Off?
Since March 2024, Reddit stock has fallen more than 40% over 30 trading days three times. The latest, on November 2, 2026, came partway through this slide. Exxon Mobil Stock Has Moved Against The Market
In the year to November 17, 2026, Exxon Mobil stock tended to move against the S&P 500. On the average day when the index rose 0.67%, a $10,000 holding in Exxon lost about $33. On the average day when the index fell 0.63%, that holding gained about $66.
Exxon therefore steadied a market portfolio rather than adding to its risk. The stock recorded a beta of minus 0.56. Beta measures how far the stock moves when the index moves. A negative beta means the shares moved the other way on average.
You received this offset alongside wider swings in Exxon itself. Its volatility, how widely its daily moves spread over a year, stood at 27.1%, compared with 13.8% for the index. Exxon did not offset every bad day. On November 5, 2026, the index’s worst day of that year, Exxon fell 2.3% while the S&P 500 fell 4.4%.

Over the five years since November 9, 2021, Exxon returned 24.6% a year including dividends. The S&P 500 returned 10.9% a year. Exxon’s annual volatility over those five years sat at 26.7%, against 17.2% for the index.
Dividing the return by the volatility reveals how much return each unit of swing earned. Exxon generated 0.92, against 0.63 for the S&P 500. The stock swung more than the market, but it paid you better for each swing.

On its October 30, 2026 earnings call, management said Middle East conflict had constrained supplies of crude, diesel and gasoline. Management said this lack of supply led to higher market prices. Exxon’s results are tied to fuel markets that management itself cannot call. That uncertainty could keep the stock’s swings wide. The direction of those swings is less settled. Exxon is expected to report in January 2027. The earnings of its Energy Products business are the number to watch.

So who pays? Someone has to find about $6 trillion of new spending a year. Anthropic’s IPO filing, amended Tuesday, points to a pool that big. Where Does Nvidia’s Money Come From?
Nvidia sells to the companies building AI data centers. They include Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle and CoreWeave. So roughly $1 of every $7 the buyers take in reaches Nvidia.

It targets Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Virginia and Wyoming.

The Trump administration has encouraged states to seek federal waivers restricting what kinds of purchases can be made with SNAP, which has traditionally allowed recipients broad autonomy to select their own groceries.

Hawaii’s waiver restricts only the purchases of soft drinks, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. But Florida’s waiver restricts purchases of soda, energy drinks, candy and prepared desserts.

I believe AI poses a significant market risk, but I'm not selling my technology stocks.

Key Points
- I vividly remember the dot-com bubble and its aftermath.

The number one thing I don't want to do, at any time and for any reason, is change my long-term investment approach to fit the current market zeitgeist. It is hard to stick to a long-term plan, especially when you believe there's a material risk of a stock market correction. But history shows that while corrections come and go, the market has always resumed its upward march.

There will be a bear market

he Trump administration is launching a new effort to combat a surge in crypto fraud and other cybercrimes targeting Americans, attacks that largely come from criminal networks located overseas.
The newly formed Threat Disruption Center will operate as a technology resource and collaboration hub for the Homeland Security Task Force, the administration said Wednesday. The center, which is comprised of more than 30 federal agencies and more than 440 state and local partners, will provide tools to address complaints from scam victims and map the networks behind the criminal operations.
The effort is being established pursuant to an executive order Trump issued in March that directed government agencies to develop a response to cybercrime and fraud that are “draining American families of their life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work and destroying the lives of our youth.”
The center will “identify victims, trace victim funds back to bad actors, identify the crypto wallets utilized both by those bad actors, and then ultimately try to identify other victims,” said Eric Weindorf, deputy director of the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center.
As part of the new effort, the government is paying TRM Labs Inc. about $95 million to provide technical support, including an artificial intelligence platform that will serve as its primary investigative tool. More than 60 TRM employees are working on the project.
“We’re looking at how can we use AI to triage victim reports in more near real time and surface opportunities where very quick action on behalf of the government could return funds to victims,” said Esteban Castaño, chief executive of TRM.
Victims in the US and abroad told the Federal Bureau of Investigation that they lost almost $21 billion to cybercrime last year, a roughly 25% surge from the previous year. Crypto-related losses accounted for more than half of that total.
The surge in fraud has posed a challenge to local law enforcement officials, in part because much of it originates overseas. It is also nearly impossible to retrieve stolen funds, which are often converted into cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin or Tether.
An outlier is the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office, which three years ago established the Virtual Currency Unit to respond to an onslaught of fraud. Run by assistant district attorney Alona Katz, the unit recently seized and disrupted more than 240 crypto-fraud websites and 112 computer servers controlled by an Eastern European fraud group, which the Brooklyn DA’s office said was “one of the biggest operational cyber disruptions undertaken by a local prosecutors’ office.”
“The Brooklyn DAs office is one of the country’s pioneers in going after these threats,” Castaño said. The Threat Disruption Center will apply the approach “across the federal government,” he said.
The government awarded the one-year agreement to TRM in July without putting it up for competitive bidding. One of TRM’s rivals, Chainalysis, sued the Trump administration, alleging that the contract awarding process was “arbitrary, capricious and unreasonable.” The lawsuit was dismissed in September.
